passage: The mock test results went up on the coaching centre's board in Jaipur at six, and Rajni was there at five-fifty. She scanned for her name at the top. It was second. Second, by one mark. Her ears rang. Vishal Sir, the physics teacher everyone feared and admired, walked past and said, "Good work, Rajni." It should have felt good. Instead she only heard the word second. That night she skipped dinner, pinned the rank list above her desk and planned four extra hours of problems a day. Her mother knocked at one a.m. "Sleep, beta. You're more than a rank." Rajni didn't look up. "Not yet," she said. "Not until I'm first."

qa.q: Where did the mock test results go up?
qa.a: On the coaching centre's board in Jaipur.

qa.q: Why did Vishal Sir's praise not feel good to Rajni?
qa.a: Rajni measured her worth by coming first, so being second by one mark made her feel she had failed despite the praise.

qa.q: What could Rajni's mother try that might help more than a late-night knock?
qa.a: She could choose a calm moment to talk about how proud she is of Rajni's effort, and help plan rest time, not just urge sleep at one a.m.

qa.q: How might Rajni's mother feel when Rajni says 'Not until I'm first'?
qa.a: Her mother may feel worried and sad that Rajni ties her worth so tightly to rank and leaves no room for rest.

grounding: A teenager's sense of worth hangs on topping the rank list and earning a respected teacher's praise, driving effort but leaving no room for rest.

passage: "Ninety-six in maths, Mummy." Elizabeth dropped her bag. "That's wonderful!" Anjali said. "Maria got ninety-eight." "So?" "So I'm not the best. Mr Joseph said he'd pick the top scorer for the Olympiad team." Anjali set down the tea. "You studied well. You understood everything." "It doesn't count unless I'm top." Elizabeth pulled out her books. "I'm redoing all the chapters tonight." "It's Friday. Your cousins are coming for dinner." "I can't, Mummy. If I relax, I'll fall behind." Anjali sat beside her. "What happens if you're not top, Liz?" Elizabeth's voice wobbled. "Then... I don't know who I am." Anjali put her arm around her and didn't say anything for a while.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth score in maths?
qa.a: Ninety-six.

qa.q: What does Elizabeth's wobbling voice suggest when she says she doesn't know who she is?
qa.a: It suggests she feels scared and fragile, as if her whole worth depends on being top.

qa.q: What could Anjali try next, after holding Elizabeth quietly?
qa.a: Anjali could help her name things she values about herself beyond marks and gently plan a rest evening, so failure feels less dangerous.

qa.q: How does Anjali seem to feel after Elizabeth's answer?
qa.a: Anjali seems moved and worried, choosing to hold her daughter quietly rather than argue.

grounding: A family scene shows a teenager who counts herself worthy only when she is top, pushing hard and refusing rest.

subtopic: Schwartz values: stimulation, achievement, power, security, conformity, tradition
passage: I'm Sahil, and in class eleven my whole life was a scoreboard. I counted everything: rank in class, number of prizes, how many times Dolma Ma'am, our chemistry teacher, said "excellent" to me versus the others. When she praised my project in assembly, I felt ten feet tall for a whole day. When I came fourth in the district quiz, I didn't speak at dinner. I studied on Diwali. I studied at my cousin's wedding, on the stairs. It worked, in a way. My marks were great. But one night I cried over a B in a practical, and I couldn't explain why to anyone. That was the first time I wondered if I was only my results.

qa.q: How did Sahil feel when Dolma Ma'am praised the project in assembly?
qa.a: Sahil felt ten feet tall for a whole day.

qa.q: What does crying over a B in a practical suggest about Sahil's state of mind?
qa.a: It suggests Sahil felt worth depended on results, so even a small dip felt like a big loss that Sahil couldn't explain.

qa.q: What turning point does Sahil describe, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Sahil began to wonder whether a person is only their results, which is the first step toward making room for rest and failure.

qa.q: How might Sahil's family have seen the studying on Diwali and at the wedding?
qa.a: They might have felt proud of the effort but also worried and a little hurt that Sahil couldn't enjoy family moments.

grounding: A teenager recalls measuring self-worth by ranks and a respected teacher's praise, fuelling effort but crowding out rest.

subtopic: Schwartz values: stimulation, achievement, power, security, conformity, tradition
passage:
Chess club note, Saturday. Nikita Joshi, coach.
Gautam (16) is my hardest worker. He tracks his rating every day on a chart taped inside his notebook. When the district secretary praised him last month, he glowed for a week. He wants first place at the state juniors, and he has told me more than once that second "doesn't count."
This week he lost a game he should have drawn. He didn't cry. He went very still, packed up without shaking hands properly, and came in the next morning with red eyes, saying he had played through the night. He has skipped every rest day I've set.
I admire his drive. It has taken him far. But I worry that he only feels he is worth something when the chart goes up.
Next: I will play one game a week with him with no rating and no result recorded, and I will talk to his parents about sleep before the tournament.

qa.q: Where does Gautam track his rating?
qa.a: On a chart taped inside his notebook.

qa.q: What does Gautam's saying that second 'doesn't count' reveal about how he sees himself?
qa.a: It reveals that he measures his worth by results, so anything less than first leaves him crushed rather than proud of his progress.

qa.q: Which of Nikita Joshi's next steps might help Gautam most, and why?
qa.a: The unrated weekly game might help most, because it lets him enjoy chess without his worth riding on the result, giving room for rest and loss.

qa.q: How might Gautam's opponent have felt when Gautam packed up without shaking hands properly?
qa.a: The opponent might have felt uneasy or slighted, not knowing how heavily the loss weighed on Gautam.

grounding: It shows a teenager who pushes for top results and praise, feeling worthy only when he wins, which drives effort but leaves no room for rest or failure.

subtopic: Schwartz values: stimulation, achievement, power, security, conformity, tradition
passage:
Friday night
Second prize. SECOND. At the district science fair, my water-filter model came second to a solar cooker. The principal shook the winner's hand and said, "This is the future." To me she said, "Good effort."
Good effort. I worked till two every night for three weeks. I skipped Parul's birthday. I didn't even go down for dinner half the time.
On the bus back I stared out of the window so nobody would see my face. Parul sat next to me and said, "Vasudha, it's a great model. You're more than a trophy." I nodded but I didn't believe her. If I'm not first, what am I?
Mumma made my favourite kadhi tonight and called me her clever girl. I couldn't eat it.
I know I'm tired. My head aches. But the inter-state fair is in four months, and I've already started planning version two.
Vasudha

qa.q: What did Vasudha's model come second to?
qa.a: A solar cooker.

qa.q: Why couldn't Vasudha believe Parul's words on the bus?
qa.a: She measures her worth by being first, so coming second made her feel like nothing, whatever her friend said.

qa.q: What choice could Vasudha make before starting version two, and why might it help?
qa.a: She could rest and eat properly for a while, and let herself enjoy the model she made, so her effort doesn't cost her sleep, friends and health.

qa.q: How might Parul feel after Vasudha skipped her birthday and then didn't believe her comfort?
qa.a: Parul might feel hurt and helpless, caring about Vasudha but unable to reach past her need to win.

grounding: It shows a teenager who feels her worth through first place and praise from respected people, pushing hard but leaving no room for rest or failure.
